Sampling plan MEG data during evening naps have been obtained from 21 participants. Data inclusion and exclusion criteria are defined in the 'Data Inclusion and Exclusion Rules' subsection. Data from two participants were used for the pilot analyses in Stage 1 and will be excluded from the planned confirmatory analyses in Stage 2, but will be included in exploratory analyses in Stage 2. Ten participants who meet the inclusion criteria will be included in the confirmatory analyses in Stage 2. The outcome will be scaled using the residual standard deviation estimated from the pilot data. Accordingly, the prior for the fixed State effect will be defined on this pilot-scaled outcome, using a zero-centered normal distribution with a standard deviation of 0.5, specified to favor relatively small effects while allowing effects in either direction. Because the scaling factor is determined solely from the pilot data, the corresponding prior scale on the original outcome scale will be fixed independently of the confirmatory data.

Posterior distributions of the model parameters will be estimated using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS; Hoffman & Gelman, 2014) implemented in PyMC (Abril-Pla et al., 2023).

A two-sided Bayes factor will be approximated using the Savage-Dickey density ratio (Wagenmakers et al., 2010), comparing the prior and posterior densities at zero under the continuous alternative model. Directional Bayes factors will then be derived according to the posterior probability of the hypothesized direction of the State effect: negative for Hypotheses 1 and 3 and positive for Hypotheses 2 and 4.

Rationale for deciding the sensitivity of the test for confirming or disconfirming the hypothesis Sensitivity analyses will be conducted using alternative priors for the fixed State effect, with standard deviations of 0.35, 0.75, and 1.0 times the residual standard deviation estimated from the pilot data. 272 Interpretation given different outcomes We will use Bayesian hypothesis testing to draw conclusions regarding the hypotheses, following the guidelines for neuroscience proposed by Keysers et al. (2020). The results will be interpreted based on directional Bayes factors (BFdir), where BFdir denotes BF_₀ for Hypotheses 1 and 3 and BF+₀ for Hypotheses 2 and 4, as follows: BFdir ≥ 10: Strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis3 ≤ BFdir < 10: Moderate evidence for the alternative hypothesis 1/3 ≤ BFdir < 3: Insufficient evidence to draw a conclusion 1/10 ≤ BFdir < 1/3: Moderate evidence for the null hypothesis BFdir < 1/10: Strong evidence for the null hypothesis Conclusions regarding the registered hypotheses will be based on the primary prior, with a standard deviation of 0.5 times the pilot residual standard deviation, whereas the sensitivity analyses will be used to assess the robustness of the evidence to reasonable alternative prior widths. Theory that could be shown wrong by the outcomes If a given hypothesis (Hypotheses 1-4) is not supported, power in the corresponding frequency range within the specified brain region will not be interpreted as a neural correlate of hypnagogic experiences during evening naps.

Methods

Since data collection has been completed, methods related to data collection are described in the past tense, while those related to the planned analyses are presented in the future tense in Stage 1 manuscript.

Participants

Participants in good physical and mental health were recruited from students at Kyushu University. Twenty-one participants (22.5 ± 2.9 years old, eight females) were selected from respondents who were not engaged in night shift work and were not wearing orthodontic appliances. Participants were instructed to wake up a few hours earlier than usual on the morning of the experiment, to refrain from consuming caffeinated beverages on the day of the experiment, and to eat supper before attending the session. They received monetary compensation after the experiment. The study was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of the Faculty of Design, Kyushu University (approval no. 598-2), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Procedure

The experiment was conducted in the evening at the Brain Center of Kyushu

Targeted Serial Awakenings and Interviews

The participants' sleep stages were monitored in real time using EEG and EOG, displayed on a monitor in the MEG control room, located next to the shielded room.

Most awakenings occurred during Hori EEG stages 4-6 of the N1. The timing of awakening was determined based on online visual inspection by the data collection team, focusing on theta activity and vertex sharp waves at Cz, which are the signs of the Hori EEG stages 4-6, where hypnagogic experiences are most likely expected (Hori et al., 1994; Tanaka et al., 1996). The experimenter awakened the participant with a brief beep when one of the following EEG patterns was visually identified on the ongoing EEG display, based on the experimenter's judgment rather than an automated threshold: (1) EEG flattening (Hori EEG stage 4), (2) continuous burst suppression of theta activity lasting several seconds (Hori EEG stage 5), or (3) a solitary vertex sharp wave (Hori EEG stage 6), predominantly at the Cz electrode. Following each awakening, the experimenter conducted a semi-structured interview to obtain reports of their conscious experiences immediately prior to awakening. Thus, our protocol was systematic and predominantly expected to yield 'experience' reports, in contrast to the serial-awakening paradigm with pseudorandom intervals adopted by Siclari et al. (2017), which yielded a more balanced distribution of 'dream experience' (42 %), 'no experience' (39 %), and 'dream experience without recall' (19 %) data.

The semi-structured interview began by asking participants whether they had been dreaming. A familiar term, 'dreaming,' was used for participants instead of specialized terminology such as 'hypnagogic experience' or 'conscious experience' for ease of understanding, and participants were provided with a list of semi-structured interview questions (Appendix 1) prior to the experiment. If they had, they were asked to freely report the content of their experience, and were then asked about the presence of colors, objects, landscapes, visual motion, self-motion, language, strangeness, and emotions, as well as details of those aspects. The participant remained stationary with their head in the MEG helmet during the interview and communicated through an intercom with the interviewer. While interviews were brief (~20 s) when participants reported no experience or were unable to recall experiential contents, when detailed contents were reported, the interview lasted approximately 3-5 min (until the participant finished reporting all experiences to their satisfaction). At the end of each interview, participants were instructed to return to sleep. An interval of at least 60 s was maintained between the end of an interview (i.e., sleep onset) and subsequent awakening. This process was continued until the end of the 2-hour MEG recording session. When sleep rapidly progressed into deeper stages, making experiences difficult to recall and subjective reports unclear, participants were awakened at intervals less than 60 s to prevent further progression of sleep stage. This procedure was applied to ~4% of awakenings.

Subjective reports were classified as follows. 1) 'Experience': when participants reported being asleep prior to awakening and recalled specific experiential content. 2) 'No experience': when they reported being asleep but recalled no experiential content upon awakening. 3) 'No recall': when they reported being asleep and indicated having had an experience but were unable to recall its content. 4) 'Not asleep': when they reported being awake at the time of awakening (despite the EEG recording indicating that they were asleep). 5) 'Unsure if dreaming' or 6) 'unsure if asleep': when participants were uncertain about their experience or sleep state.

more days (see Table 2). 368 of each type of subjective report for each Hori EEG stage, scored offline by two 384 members of the data acquisition team (TT and CHI) based on the final 5 s before awakening, following the criteria of Hori et al. (1994).

For comparison with previous studies, standard sleep staging was performed based on the final 30 s before awakening. Sleep stages preceding each awakening were determined using U-Sleep, a deep learning-based algorithm for automated clinical sleep staging (Perslev et al., 2021). This algorithm leverages large datasets to classify polysomnography (PSG) data according to AASM guidelines (Berry et al., 2017).

Staging was performed using the U-Sleep Web API Python binding with the U-Sleep-FT v2.0 model, which had been trained on 16 clinical cohorts and 25,696 PSG records.

A 30-second anonymized PSG, recorded from three EEG electrodes (Fz, Cz, and Pz) and EOG from both eyes in our experiment, was used to determine sleep stages.

Data Inclusion and Exclusion Rules

Data segments contaminated by evident artifacts, such as large body movements or interruptions due to external loud sounds during the nap, will be excluded prior to preprocessing. Table 3 shows the number of awakenings without evident artifacts for each participant, categorized by subjective report type across experimental days.

According to the U-Sleep classification based on 30-s EEG and EOG data recorded prior to awakening, 28% of awakenings were classified as stage N1 and 15% as stage N2 (see Table 4). A small number of awakenings during stage N3 yielded no recallable reports. In addition, 34% of awakenings were classified as wake, likely because awakening timing was determined by visually monitoring EEG and EOG signals during the several seconds preceding each awakening. The standard sleep stage classification, based on 30-s windows and a limited number of electrodes, is relatively coarse and may overlook subtle spatiotemporal changes in brain activity during the hypnagogic state.

In addition, it has been suggested that individuals can report dream-like mental content even when their state is classified as wakefulness using the standard method (Lacaux et al., 2024; Nielsen, 2017). Therefore, all awakenings associated with experience or no-experience reports will be included regardless of the sleep stage assigned by U-Sleep. It is currently unclear whether the neural correlates of consciousness are consistent across sleep stages, and pooling data across stages may the State effect. We acknowledge these issues as limitations of the confirmatory 419 analyses. To account for day-to-day fluctuations in baseline neural states, only data 420 from experimental days on which both experience and no-experience states were 421 reported will be included for each participant. Accordingly, participants who did not 422 report both states on at least one experimental day will be excluded from the 423 confirmatory analyses. This criterion is consistent with Experiment 2 of Siclari et al. 424 (2017). Awakenings associated with other subjective states, such as 'no recall', will be 425 excluded to ensure a clear contrast between experience and no-experience states. 426 Therefore, data from ten participants will be available for the confirmatory analyses 427 in Stage 2, excluding Participants 5 and 11, whose data were used in the pilot analyses, 428 as shown in Table 3. Across participants included in the confirmatory analyses, the 429 number of experience reports ranged from 9 to 50, whereas the number of no-430 experience reports ranged from 1 to 11.431

Simulation-based Sample-size Analysis

Because the cryogenic MEG system at the data-collection site was discontinued, data collection had already been completed before we were able to conduct an a priori sample-size analysis, and no additional data can be collected. Nevertheless, we conducted a simulation-based sample-size analysis using the Bayesian linear mixedeffects model planned for the confirmatory analyses.

For the simulations, the expected population-level State effects were informed by effect sizes derived from the t-statistics reported for the delta and low-gamma frequency bands in the posterior hot zone during NREM sleep in Supplementary Figure 5 of Siclari et al. (2017). Pilot data from two participants were used to inform the residual and random-effects variance components. In addition, the observed distribution of experience and no-experience awakenings across participant-days was used to represent the distribution expected in the confirmatory analyses.

Under the assumptions of the simulation, N = 33 was estimated to be sufficient to achieve a probability of at least 0.80 of obtaining strong directional evidence (BFdir ≥ 10) for each of the two primary hypotheses (Hypotheses 1 and 2), based on 500 simulated datasets per candidate sample size. Using the same simulations, N = 28 was estimated to be sufficient to achieve P(BFdir ≥ 3) ≥ 0.80 for each of the two primary hypotheses.

We will conduct the registered analyses using the available sample (N=10) and report the resulting directional Bayes factors, while acknowledging the limited probability of obtaining moderate or strong evidence under the assumptions of the simulation.

Analysis

To facilitate comparison with the results of Siclari et al. (2017), we will use the same parameters, such as the time window for analysis. However, necessary methodological adjustments will be made to accommodate the current dataset, given technical differences in measurement techniques (MEG vs. EEG) and sleep conditions (nap, primarily N1, vs. sleep, primarily N2 and N3).

We will analyze MEG data using MNE-Python (v.1.8.0) (Gramfort, 2013) in conjunction with FreeSurfer software, which enables co-registration with digitized head points and structural MRI data to generate a forward solution and subsequently display the reconstructed source on the cerebral surface.

Preprocessing

First, a notch filter will be applied to the raw MEG data to remove 60 Hz power-line noise. Next, a bandpass filter between 0.3 and 50 Hz will be applied to eliminate artifacts caused by drift and muscle movements. The data will then be downsampled to 500 Hz. We will apply independent component analysis (ICA) to remove residual artifacts associated with eye movements, cardiac activity, and muscle activity. For each run, we will fit ICA to the MEG channels and estimate 20 independent components using the Infomax algorithm (Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). To ensure consistent identification of artifact-related components across datasets, we will select components for exclusion using predefined statistical criteria implemented in MNE-Python.

We will identify eye movement-related components separately using the left and right EOG channels. For each channel, we will calculate Pearson correlations between the EOG signal and the ICA component time series and identify components with outlying correlation scores using MNE-Python's iterative z-scoring procedure, with an automatically selected threshold of z = 3.0.

Because we did not record ECG directly, we will generate a synthetic ECG signal in MNE-Python through cross-channel averaging of the MEG signals and use it to identify cardiac-related components. We will detect cardiac artifacts using both crosstrial phase statistics (CTPS) and correlation-based methods. For CTPS, we will identify components exceeding the automatically determined CTPS threshold for exclusion (Dammers et al., 2008). For correlation-based detection, we will calculate Pearson correlations between the synthetic ECG signal and the ICA component time series and identify outlying components.

We will identify muscle-related components using ica.find_bads_muscle, with a threshold of 0.5 and a frequency range of 7-45 Hz. We will combine components identified by any of the ECG-, EOG-, or muscle-artifact detection procedures, remove duplicates, and mark the resulting components for exclusion. We will then reconstruct the MEG data after excluding these components and segment the reconstructed data into 20-s epochs corresponding to the sleep period immediately preceding each awakening.

Regions of Interest

Based on the findings of Siclari et al. (2017) and a subsequent EEG study by Selte et al. (2026), we defined two regions of interest (ROIs): frontal and posterior. The regions included in each ROI are selected based on the Desikan-Killiany atlas, which anatomically labels 34 brain regions (Desikan et al., 2006). The frontal ROI includes the following nine regions: superior frontal, rostral middle frontal, caudal middle frontal, pars opercularis, pars triangularis, pars orbitalis, lateral orbitofrontal, medial orbitofrontal, and frontal pole. Likewise, the posterior ROI includes the following eight regions: supramarginal, superior parietal, inferior parietal, precuneus, lingual, pericalcarine, cuneus, and lateral occipital (Figure 1).

Source Reconstruction

The head model will be constructed using a single-layer boundary element model (BEM) with a conductivity of 0.3 S/m and a surface tessellation corresponding to the fourth-order subdivision of an icosahedron (ico4). The cortical source space will be defined using the sixth-order subdivision of an octahedron (oct6). We will obtain the MRI-head coordinate transformation manually by coregistering digitized fiducials and head-shape points with each participant's structural MRI. A forward solution mapping cortical source activity to MEG sensor measurements will be then computed using the BEM, source space, and the resulting transformation, with the minimum distance between sources and the inner skull surface set to 5.0 mm.

Noise covariance between channels will be estimated using MEG data recorded during a two-minute quiet period at the beginning of the first run of each session (i. e., experimental day). We will apply the noise covariance estimated from the first run to all runs acquired on the same day for a given participant. For each experimental day, an inverse operator for the minimum-norm estimate will then be computed by combining the forward model with the corresponding noise covariance, using the minimum_norm.make_inverse_operator function with default parameters. We will perform source reconstruction for each epoch using the inverse operator specific to each experimental day. The regularization parameter for the Tikhonov procedure will be set to 1/9, corresponding to a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 3. As the inverse solution method, we will use dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM) (Dale et al., 2000), although Siclari et al. (2017) employed standardized low-resolution electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA) (Pascual-Marqui, 2002). dSPM provides a noise-normalized minimum-norm estimate at each source location, making it well suited for reducing noise specific to MEG measurements across different experimental days, including differences in head-sensor distance, fluctuations in baseline brain activity, and variations in sensor signal-to-noise ratios.

Power Spectral Density

The power spectral density (PSD) of the reconstructed sources will be computed for the delta (1-4 Hz) and low-gamma (20-50 Hz) ranges for each epoch. Following the methodology of Siclari et al. (2017), we will estimate PSD using Welch's method (Welch, 1967) with a 2-s Hamming window and 50% overlap, implemented via the psd_array_welch function in MNE-Python. This procedure decomposes the reconstructed source time course into a mean PSD value within the specified frequency range. Then, we will calculate the mean PSD within each ROI for each epoch.

Statistical Analysis

For group-level hypothesis testing, we will use Bayesian linear mixed-effects models implemented in PyMC (Abril-Pla et al., 2023). We will first test the two primary hypotheses (Hypotheses 1 and 2) concerning posterior delta (1-4 Hz) and low-gamma (20-50 Hz) power, respectively. Separate models will be fitted for each frequency band.

To ensure that the scale of the prior distribution is determined independently of the confirmatory data, neural power quantified as PSD will be linearly rescaled using scaling parameters estimated exclusively from the pilot data (Participants 5 and 11).

Pilot Analysis

To assess the feasibility of our methodologies, we used data from two participants (Participants 5 and 11) for pilot analyses. These data were used because the two participants had been randomly selected by several members of the data acquisition team (YM, HT, MI, HS, KH, and CHI) for preliminary analysis, and the results were presented at the 27th annual meeting of the Association for the Scientific Study of Consciousness (ASSC27; poster available at: https://figshare.com/s/e1d1f7d52f1ca8f96ad9). None of the data analysis team members for this registered report will have access to any other data before the start of Stage 2.

We applied the same procedure planned for the critical dataset (N = 10) to the pilot data (N = 2). For the statistical analysis, we fitted Bayesian linear mixed-effects models separately for each participant, with State as a fixed effect and experimental day as a random intercept. Compared with the models planned for the confirmatory analyses, only experimental day was included as a random effect, and the neural data were standardized using the mean and standard deviation calculated within each participant.

Timeline

Upon acceptance of the first stage of this registered report, data from all participants will be shared with the analysis team, which will then proceed with analyzing the remaining dataset. We expect to take approximately one year to summarize the results, write the discussion, and finalize the Stage 2 report following in-principle acceptance.

Data and Code Availability

MEG, EEG, and EOG data, together with subjective reports, will be made available as part of the DREAM database (Wong et al., 2025) at (https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/MEG_Kyushu/27116590) upon completion of the relevant research associated with this study. Structural MRI data will be shared upon reasonable request, in accordance with personal data protection regulations. Python scripts, metadata, and pilot result data are available at (https://github.com/hc21-rgb/consciousness-meg-analysis).

These correspond to prior standard deviations of 0.35spilot, 0.75sspilot, and 1.0sspilot, respectively, on the original PSD scale. Conclusions will be based on the primary prior with a standard deviation of 0.5, whereas the sensitivity analyses will be used to assess the robustness of the evidence to reasonable alternative prior widths.

Posterior distributions will be estimated using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS; Hoffman & Gelman, 2014), an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithm implemented in PyMC. We will run four independent chains, each with 6,000 tuning iterations followed by 6,000 post-warm-up draws. We will set the target acceptance probability to 0.99 and assess convergence and sampling quality using rank-normalized 𝑅 V , bulk and tail effective sample sizes (ESSs), and divergent transitions. We will require 𝑅 V < 1.01, bulk and tail ESSs of at least 400 for parameters relevant to hypothesis testing, and no divergent transitions. Pilot analyses indicated that these sampling settings were sufficient to achieve satisfactory convergence and sampling quality.

We will use directional Bayes factors to quantify evidence for each hypothesis relative to the point null hypothesis of no State effect.

For each analysis, a two-sided Bayes factor will first be approximated using the Savage-Dickey density ratio (Wagenmakers et al., 2010): .

Here, p(β₁ = 0 | H₁) denotes the prior density at zero under the continuous alternative model, and p(β₁ = 0 | data, H₁) denotes the corresponding posterior density at zero. The posterior density at zero will be estimated from the posterior draws of β₁ using kernel density estimation.

For Hypothesis 1, the directional alternative hypothesis is corresponding to lower posterior delta power during experience than during noexperience.

List of Semi-Structured Interview Questions

Were you dreaming?

If the answer was 'yes,' the participant was asked the following:

Please describe the contents of the dream.

Depending on the participant's description, further questions were asked:

Did you see anything?

Did you see colors vividly?

If the participant mentioned seeing colors, they were asked:

What object had what color?

Was there any movement in the images?

Did you hear anything?

Did you feel any body movement or a sensation of floating?

Did you experience any other sensations?

Were there any humans in the dream?

Were there any words or language?

Was there anything else you haven't mentioned?

Did anything feel strange during the dream?

Did you experience any emotions?

If 'yes,' the participant was asked:

How intense were those emotions?

If the participant responded other than 'yes' to the first question, the following questions were asked:

Were you dreaming but unable to remember the content?

Were you asleep?

Were you awake and thinking?

Were you awake without thinking?

Note that the questions were always presented in the same sequential order, and the list of interview questions was explained to participants before they went to sleep.

The model can be expressed asy ~ State + (1 + State || Participant) + (1 | Participant : Day)where y denotes neural power quantified as PSD. The fixed intercept represents the population-level mean neural power averaged across the experience and no-experience states, and the fixed State effect represents the population-level difference in neural power between the two states. Participant-specific random intercepts and random slopes for State will be modeled as independent, and random intercepts for experimental days will be nested within participants.

University Hospital. Prior to the MEG measurement, electrodes for electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG), as well as head position indicator (HPI) coils for MEG, were placed on the participants' scalp and face. After digitizing anatomical fiducials, head-shape points, and HPI coil locations using a Polhemus digitizing system, and after receiving detailed instructions about the experiment, participants lay supine in a magnetically shielded room with their heads positioned in the MEG helmet. Participants then began their nap. Each session typically commenced around 7 p.m. and lasted up to two hours, in accordance with the protocol approved by the Ethics Review Committee. Recording MEG signals were recorded using the Neuromag system (Elekta / MEGIN), which consists of 306 channels: 204 planar gradiometers and 102 magnetometers. EEG signals from Fz, Cz, and Pz, following the international 10-20 system, and EOG signals from both left canthus and below the right eye, covering both left and right eye movements, were simultaneously recorded with passive electrodes. The ground electrode was attached to the forehead, and the EEG and EOG signals were referenced to the left earlobe. The impedance of the electrodes was checked to be below 15 kΩ before the recording. The MEG system concurrently recorded MEG, EEG, and EOG data. All data were recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. Participants remained in a supine position throughout the recording. The head location relative to the MEG sensors was recorded using four HPI coils, which were attached above the left and right eyebrows and the left and right mastoids. Recording generally continued for up to twohours. However, if participants requested a pause to make the nap condition more comfortable, such as by taking a blanket, the session recording was split into multiple runs. Maxfilter (Elekta, version 2.2) was applied to the MEG raw data to mitigate external magnetic interference.

For Participant 11, the single-participant Bayesian linear mixed-effects model indicated that delta power tended to be lower in the experience state than in the no-experience state, as reflected by a negative State effect (β1 =-0.0013). Although the 95% highest density interval (HDI) included zero, most of the posterior distribution was below zero (95% HDI: [-0.0028, 0.00019]), with a posterior probability of P(β₁ < 0 | data) = 0.95. The directional Bayes factor provided moderate evidence in the hypothesized direction (BF-0 = 4.94). In contrast, the same analysis of low-gamma power provided insufficient evidence for the hypothesized increase in the experience state (β1 =-0.000021, 95% HDI: [-0.00015, 0.00011], P(β₁ > 0 | data) = 0.37, BF +0 = 0.36). For Participant 5, the same analyses provided insufficient evidence for the hypothesized effects for both delta power (β1 = 0.0013, 95% HDI: [-0.011, 0.013], P(β₁ < 0 | data) = 0.42, BF-0 = 0.57) and low-gamma power (β1 = -0.0000067, 95% HDI: [-0.0010, 0.00099], P(β₁ > 0 | data) = 0.51, BF+0 = 0.62). The secondary Hypotheses 3 and 4 predict that, within the frontal ROI, delta power is lower and low-gamma power is higher, respectively, in the experience state than in the no-experience state. 35, BF-0 = 0.55) and low-gamma power (β1 = -0.0000056, 95% HDI: [-0.00044, 0.00042], P(β₁ > 0 | data) = 0.49, BF+0 = 0.64). MCMC sampling showed satisfactory convergence for the State effect, with 𝑅 V < 1.01, and both bulk and tail effective sample sizes (ESSs) of at least 400 in all analyses, supporting the feasibility of the planned modeling approach. We also assessed the feasibility of the confirmatory analysis by applying the planned group-level Bayesian linear mixed-effects models to the pilot data from Participants 5 and 11. The models achieved satisfactory convergence with 6,000 tuning iterations followed by 6,000 post-warm-up draws and a target acceptance probability of 0.99. We will therefore use these sampling parameters for the confirmatory analyses. Because the pilot dataset included only two participants, these analyses were intended primarily to assess the feasibility of fitting the planned models rather than to provide reliable estimates of population-level State effects. Consistent with this limitation, the models provided insufficient evidence for the hypothesized effects in all four analyses: posterior delta power (β1 = -0.00022, 95% HDI: [-0.0065, 0.0060], P(β₁ < 0 | data) =

53, BF-0 = 0.71), posterior low-gamma power (β1 = -0.0000031, 95% HDI: [-0.00048,

00047], P(β₁ > 0 | data) = 0.49, BF+0 = 0.64), frontal delta power (β1 = -0.00021, 95% HDI: [-0.0047, 0.0041], P(β₁ < 0 | data) = 0.54, BF-0 = 0.74), and frontal low-gamma power (β1 = 0.00000081, 95% HDI: [-0.00024, 0.00025], P(β₁ > 0 | data) = 0.50, BF+0 = 0.65).
